## F2: the exact class is included, without admitting nonintegrable exceptions

For a finite product in F3, the polynomial factor at real infinity is asymptotic to `|x|^(2 sum alpha)` times a positive constant. If a<0, the positive quartic exponential overwhelms every other factor and prevents integrability. If a=0 and b<=0, the source is either growing exponentially or asymptotic to a nonnegative power, again not integrable. Thus integrability indeed implies a>=0, and when a=0 it implies b>0. No contrary tail cancellation is available because all exponents are nonnegative and every factor is positive away from zero.

For all such integrable finite products,

    log rho(s)=log A-a s^2-b s+sum alpha log(s+lambda),
    (log rho)''=-2a-sum alpha/(s+lambda)^2<=0,
    (log rho)'''=2sum alpha/(s+lambda)^3>=0.

The formulas remain valid for lambda=0 on the stipulated domain s>0. The value assigned at x=0 has no role in the Fourier probability law. The third finite-difference inequality follows by the previously checked compact-cube integral identity. Positive scalar normalization changes only log A, so both invariants survive.

The number of factors, their rates and exponents, and the Gaussian/quartic coefficients may vary without uniform bounds. For the infinite-limit entrance, positive finite pointwise limits preserve log concavity by passing to the defining three-value concavity inequality; they preserve the third log-difference inequality by passing to its four values. Subsequent normalization by a positive finite mass preserves both. No convergence of derivatives or normalization constants is needed for this finite-value argument.

The candidate correctly restricts these inherited properties to the stated class and, generally, to profiles satisfying BOTH F2 invariants. It does not import log concavity from an arbitrary pointwise limit of the earlier enlarged nonintegrable comparison class with negative a. The old normalized Gaussian*sinh-product sibling is included by its convergent positive finite products. Integrability and positivity of the final q_j are explicit requirements rather than consequences silently assumed for every limit.

## F3: Fourier signs, test functions, and local measure convergence

For the stated convention

    hat psi(t)=integral exp(-itx)psi(x)dx,
    F_j(t)=integral exp(itx)q_j(x)dx,

Fourier inversion gives the exact pairing

    integral psi(x)q_j(x)dx
      =(1/(2pi))integral hat psi(t)F_j(t)dt.

There is no conjugation or minus sign missing. Because q_j is a nonnegative probability density, `|F_j(t)|<=1` for every real t. The transform of a compact smooth test is integrable. Fubini is therefore absolutely justified, and dominated convergence under the assumed pointwise convergence on the entire real Fourier axis gives the analogous test pairing for the actual q.

This step uses neither a Levy continuity theorem nor tightness, a uniform moment bound, a uniform source tail estimate, or convergence of Fourier derivatives. Nonnegativity and the common mass bound provide the entire domination needed here. The target is the probability-normalized actual q and its corresponding Fourier transform F, so there is no mismatch with F_j(0)=1.

For phi in C_c^infinity((0,infinity)), its support is a positive distance from zero. Thus `psi(x)=|x|phi(x^2)` vanishes near zero and is genuinely smooth and compactly supported on the real line. Evenness yields

    integral_R |x|phi(x^2)q_j(x)dx
      =2 integral_0^infinity x phi(x^2)q_j(x)dx
      =integral_0^infinity phi(s)rho_j(s)ds.

Here ds=2x dx cancels the factor two exactly. The same identity holds for q. Consequently rho_j(s)ds converges to rho(s)ds against every smooth compact test on the open positive half-line. No bound on their total masses, which would involve a source moment, has been introduced.

## F4: complete local log-concavity stability proof

The supplied lemma is sound for positive continuous p_j and a positive continuous limiting density p on an open interval. It does not require global normalization of these interval measures.

Fix a nondegenerate compact interval K inside I. Choose L strictly to its left and R strictly to its right, as in the candidate. Nonnegative smooth tests supported in the two intervals have positive limiting integrals. For all sufficiently large j their integrals are uniformly bounded below. Dividing by the fixed positive test masses shows that there are u_j in L and v_j in R with both p_j values at least one fixed c>0. This inference uses positivity and compactness, not an a priori bound on p_j.

Concavity of log p_j bounds p_j below by c along the segment from u_j to v_j. One may choose a single fixed [a,b] between L and R, with K inside its interior; the lower bound then holds throughout [a,b], including both endpoints. A nonnegative compact smooth test at least one on [a,b] gives, by test convergence, a uniform upper bound C for the mass of that entire interval.

For x in [a,b], put M=p_j(x)>=c and choose the more distant endpoint y. The segment length is at least d=(b-a)/2. On the unoriented segment between x and y, log concavity gives

    C >= integral_(min(x,y))^(max(x,y)) p_j
      >= d integral_0^1 M^t c^(1-t)dt
      = d (M-c)/log(M/c), M>c.

The expression tends continuously to dc at M=c and tends to infinity as M tends to infinity. It therefore gives a uniform upper bound for every height M on [a,b]. In particular both upper and lower bounds for log p_j on this entire larger interval have now been derived from local test convergence.

For completeness, if the oscillation of log p_j on [a,b] is bounded by B and K has distance at least delta>0 from both endpoints, the secant-slope inequalities for concave functions bound every slope between two points of K between -B/delta and B/delta. This supplies a common Lipschitz bound; differentiability is not required.

Arzela–Ascoli now applies to log p_j on K. From any subsequence one may select a further subsequence converging uniformly there to a continuous logarithm g. Uniform convergence of the exponentials and the given measure-test convergence imply

    integral phi exp(g)=integral phi p

for all smooth tests supported in the interior of K. Hence exp(g)=p on that interior, and equality extends to the endpoints by continuity. Thus every subsequential uniform limit is log p. A subsequence staying a positive uniform distance away from log p would contradict its own Arzela–Ascoli sublimit; the whole sequence therefore converges uniformly in logarithm and in density on K.

The one-point case is covered by a containing nondegenerate compact interval, and arbitrary compact subsets can also be contained in such an interval. This proves the full local-uniform conclusion. All constants may depend on K and the limiting positive p. That is sufficient: no uniformity as K moves to infinity is used or needed.

## F5: contradiction, including the order of choices

Apply the lemma with p_j=rho_j and p=rho. The actual rho is positive and continuous on the entire open positive half-line, so the hypotheses hold, including on arbitrarily far but fixed compact intervals. It follows that rho_j converges locally uniformly to rho. At any fixed four-node configuration, positivity of rho makes the logarithms converge as well, and the nonnegative third difference in F2 passes to the limit.

Choose one sufficiently large R from the accepted F1 so that `Delta_R^3 log rho(R)<0`, and fix those four nodes before taking j to infinity. This contradicts the nonnegative limiting finite difference. The possibly very small source mass near those far nodes causes no gap: the lemma uses a fixed positive lower test integral for the already chosen compact set, and needs no lower bound uniform in R.

Thus no sequence of normalized nonnegative even sources with both F2 invariants can have Fourier transforms converging to the actual normalized F pointwise on the whole real axis. Locally uniform convergence as entire functions would imply that real-axis convergence and is therefore excluded as well. The proof does not assume real zeros of the approximating transforms; imposing that extra requirement cannot evade the obstruction.

This genuinely extends the previous pointwise-source exclusion for the specified normalized class. It does not retroactively attribute Fourier closure to the earlier theorem alone. The additional local stability argument is the new step, and both its hypotheses are checked here.

## Limits of the accepted conclusion

The accepted obstruction applies to the finite integrable positive products F3 with arbitrary varying parameters and to the expressly stated positive limit class satisfying F2 after normalization. It does not exclude signed sources, loss of log concavity under positive mixing, other seeds, other maps, or unrelated Fourier approximations. No preservation of real zeros is asserted for those excluded-from-scope alternatives.

The already accepted exp(-x^6) control has negative third log differences and lies outside F2, despite its real-zero Fourier transform. It remains a separate control rather than an actual-theta source or a negative original V witness. The new proof supplies no global Pick property, original V sign, RH conclusion, or new property of primes.

No missing moment or tail hypothesis, factor-of-two error, Fourier sign error, or gap in the local compactness argument was found. The only written artifact is this assigned private review. No new agents, external messages, literature hunt, numerical experiment, Lean, canonical edit, publication, or checkpoint script was used. The bounded review is complete and authorizes no additional task.

I rechecked the exact two-invariant entrance independently of the earlier
larger C2 comparison class. For finite integrable positive products a>=0

log derivative is nonpositive and the third log difference is nonnegative.

unproved derivative convergence. Sources that are not integrable or do not
have both invariants are not admitted by this theorem.

The Fourier test identity uses the positive-sign characteristic transform
and the negative-sign test transform, giving no extra conjugate or minus.
Probability normalization bounds all |F_j| by one. Fourier inversion and
integrability of the smooth test transform give the required dominated
convergence without a tail or moment assumption. The test |x|phi(x^2) is
smooth because phi is zero near zero; evenness and ds=2x dx cancel the
factor two. Only compactly supported rho-measure pairings are obtained and
only those are used.

For the local stability lemma the two anchors give a lower bound on the
whole intervening fixed interval. A test at least one there gives its mass
upper bound. Integrating the logarithmic chord from any height to the
farther endpoint bounds that height by the logarithmic mean. Bounded
concave logarithms have uniformly bounded interior secant slopes, so
Arzela--Ascoli applies. Each continuous limit is uniquely identified by
the same compact test pairings, which yields convergence of the full
sequence. The constants may deteriorate far in the tail, but a single
large R is fixed before taking the approximation limit; no uniformity in R
is required for the four-node contradiction.

Consequently real-axis pointwise Fourier convergence, hence entire local
uniform convergence, is impossible for this exact normalized nonnegative
class. No real-zero assumption on the approximants is needed. The result
closes an explicit loophole left by the prior report; it does not prove
anything about original V's sign, actual Pick, or RH. The known w6 control
still lies outside the invariant class and prevents an overgeneralization.

No correction was required. No new literature mechanism, arithmetic input,
Lean proof, numerical test, source-sign counter reset or canonical admission
is claimed. Publish the isolated report and its exact review certificate;
synchronize once in the living Proshka chat. No new proof request for this
excluded approximation class is justified.
